01-cua-song-bach-dang: Wide high view over the Bạch Đằng estuary in winter, flat cool light: a very wide brown tidal river opening to the sea, muddy banks with mangroves and reeds, limestone karst islets in the distance. On the water, the tops of hundreds of sharpened wooden stakes stick up in rows across the river, and among them a few broken Southern Han war junks tilt and sink. Small Vietnamese boats with fighters row between them. Calm after battle, no bodies, no blood.
02-nam-937: A quiet scene in the governor's residence of Tĩnh Hải in the year 937, daytime: a wooden hall with a tiled roof, a courtyard with a tree and a small pond. DƯƠNG ĐÌNH NGHỆ sits reading documents at a low table, a few guards at the door. Peaceful, ordinary day, before trouble.
03-kieu-cong-tien: Night in light blue-grey tones lit by lanterns, clearly readable. In the corridor of the governor's residence, KIỀU CÔNG TIỄN, in a black robe, leads a few armed men in dark clothes creeping toward a lit doorway, his face scheming, a sword half drawn. Tense, sinister mood. The act itself is NOT shown: no blood, no body, no stabbing.
04-ngo-quyen-xuat-quan: Daytime, a Vietnamese army sets out along a dirt road through rice fields: a column of fighters with spears, sabres and rattan shields, banners of plain dark cloth with no writing. At the head on a horse rides NGÔ QUYỀN, stern and determined, pointing forward. Hills behind.
05-cau-cuu-nam-han: Inside the Southern Han court, daytime: red lacquered pillars, plain red hangings with no writing. A Vietnamese envoy sent by KIỀU CÔNG TIỄN kneels low and presents a sealed bamboo letter tube. The Southern Han emperor Lưu Cung, a stout Han Chinese man with a beard in a yellow-and-black robe and a crown, sits on a throne looking interested, officials in dark robes on both sides.
06-tru-kieu-cong-tien: Daytime in the courtyard of the governor's residence, now taken by NGÔ QUYỀN's men. NGÔ QUYỀN stands tall at the top of the steps, hand on his sabre hilt. Below him KIỀU CÔNG TIỄN kneels with his hands bound behind his back, head bowed, guarded by two Vietnamese soldiers. Autumn leaves on the ground. No execution shown, no blood.
07-thuy-quan-nam-han: Daytime at sea, wide view: a large Southern Han fleet of big wooden war junks with square batten sails and painted eyes on the bows sails toward the coast in formation, plain red banners with no writing. On the deck of the leading junk stands LƯU HOẰNG THÁO in gilded armour and red cape, confident. Waves, gulls, karst islets on the horizon.
08-dong-coc: Daytime at low tide in the wide muddy Bạch Đằng river mouth. Hundreds of Vietnamese workers and soldiers drive huge sharpened wooden stakes into the riverbed in long rows, using heavy wooden mallets and ropes; the tips of the stakes are capped with dark iron points. Rafts loaded with more logs float nearby. NGÔ QUYỀN on the bank points and directs. Busy, purposeful.
09-trieu-len: Daytime, the same wide river mouth at high tide: the water is high and smooth, and the rows of stakes are completely hidden beneath the brown surface, only faint ripples where they stand. A few Vietnamese scouts in a small boat glance down at the water knowingly. Mangroves on the banks half submerged. Calm, deceptive.
10-khieu-chien: Daytime on the river at high tide. A handful of small, light Vietnamese boats paddled by fighters row toward the huge Southern Han war junks, waving spears and banners to provoke them, then turn around and paddle away as if fleeing, one fighter looking back over his shoulder with a sly grin. The big junks start to give chase.
11-duoi-vao-bai-coc: Daytime, wide view along the river. The Southern Han fleet of big war junks chases the small Vietnamese boats upstream, deeper and deeper into the river mouth, sails full. Below the water surface, drawn faintly as dark shapes, rows of hidden stakes wait right under the hulls. The junks do not see them. Tension.
12-trieu-rut: Daytime, a dramatic still moment: the tide is going out fast, the river water dropping, muddy banks widening, water rushing seaward in long flat streaks. The tips of the first dark stakes begin to break the surface between the big Southern Han junks. Sailors on deck lean over the rails, alarmed.
13-thuyen-mac-coc: Daytime, the climax of the battle at low tide: the rows of sharpened stakes now stand out of the water, and the big Southern Han war junks are impaled on them, tilted, cracked, some capsizing, sails collapsing. Small Vietnamese boats dart in among them with fighters shooting arrows and throwing spears. Splashes, splintered wood, smoke from a burning sail. No blood, no gore.
14-hoang-thao-tu-tran: Daytime, a sombre close moment on the river: a broken, sinking Southern Han flagship tilts in the water among the stakes, its red banner trailing in the river, a gilded helmet with a red plume floating on the surface beside it. No body shown, no blood. Smoke drifts over the water.
15-nam-han-rut-quan: Late afternoon, sombre warm light at sea. The few remaining Southern Han war junks, damaged with torn sails, turn away and sail back out to sea in retreat. On the shore in the foreground, Vietnamese fighters raise their spears and cheer. Karst islets on the horizon.
16-ngo-quyen-xung-vuong: Daytime, spring, a ceremony at Cổ Loa: earthen ramparts and a wooden royal hall with a tiled roof, flowering peach trees. NGÔ QUYỀN, now in a royal dark red robe and a crown, stands at the top of the hall steps while officials and soldiers bow below him. Plain banners with no writing. Festive and proud.
17-coc-go-ngay-nay: EXCEPTION: this single scene is set in the PRESENT DAY, modern things are allowed. A calm outdoor heritage site by the Bạch Đằng river at golden hour: a field of old dark wooden stakes preserved standing in the ground, a simple wooden walkway around them, a Vietnamese family looking at them, the wide river and karst islets behind. A blank sign board with NO text. Peaceful and reflective.
